Now process the following competition-level biology question:

Flow cytometry is a method for analyzing multiple cells in suspension.

Cells pass through a microfluidic system, where they are irradiated by lasers. Laser light photons are partially scattered by cells and partially absorbed by fluorophores (fluorescent molecules). Excited fluorophores then emit secondary photons at longer wave lengths.

Fluorophores are typically small organic molecules with conjugated double bonds.

- Low angle scattering is measured by a forward scattering (FSC) detector.
- High angle scattering is measured by a side scattering (SSC) detector.
- Fluorescence is measured by wavelength-specific detectors.

FSC positively correlates with cell size, while SSC positively correlates with cell-surface 'texture' and 'granularity', including protrusions, pockets and underlying vesicles.

The results of measurement are typically represented on dot-plot diagrams. Each dot represents a single-cell, with the density of dots in an area indicated by color (Red is high density, dark blue is low density).

[Figure Description: A flow cytometry dot-plot diagram with Axis X representing FSC (Forward Scatter) and Axis Y representing SSC (Side Scatter). The plot shows three distinct circled populations of cells:
- Area 1: Located at low FSC and low SSC. It has a high density of dots (red/yellow core).
- Area 2: Located at medium FSC and low SSC (to the right of Area 1). It has a medium-high density of dots.
- Area 3: Located at medium to high FSC and high SSC (above Area 2 and extending further right). It has a broad spread with medium density.
The axes have tick marks but no numerical values.]

The figure above shows flow cytometry analysis of mouse blood. Blood was pretreated with red blood cell lysis buffer.

Axis X shows FSC.
Axis Y shows SSC.

An FSC-threshold was used to exclude the particles with very low FSC from the plot (e.g. debris).

## Indicate True and False statements:

3.1 Lymphocytes are shown in Area 1.
3.2 Residual red blood cells are shown in Area 2.
3.3 Neutrophils and other granulocytes are shown in Area 3.
3.4 In general, unstained blood cells show no fluorescence.

Part A
In an experiment, soldiers were ordered to march through a hot desert until exhaustion (they were then retrieved and given a reward).
- One group (red) had no food or water.
- The second (blue) group had access to limitless water.
- The third group (black) had access to both limitless water and limitless savoury (salty, low energy) food.

Graph A shows Core body temperature (Y-axis, where a = Normal, b = Hot) versus Length of march (X-axis).
- Red curve: Starts at 'a', rises steeply towards 'b', and ends earliest.
- Blue curve: Starts at 'a', rises towards 'b' but less steeply than the red group, and ends later than the red group.
- Black curve: Starts at 'a', remains relatively flat near 'a' (rising very slightly), and ends latest.

Graph B shows Blood osmolarity (Y-axis, where a = Low, b = Medium, c = High) versus Length of march (X-axis).
- Red curve: Starts at 'b', rises steeply towards 'c', and ends earliest.
- Blue curve: Starts at 'b', drops towards 'a', and ends later than the red group.
- Black curve: Starts at 'b', remains relatively flat near 'b' (rising very slightly), and ends latest.

Graph C shows Cardiac output (Y-axis, where a = Low, b = Normal) versus Length of march (X-axis).
- Red curve: Starts at 'b', drops steeply towards 'a', and ends earliest.
- Blue curve: Starts at 'b', drops towards 'a' but less steeply than the red group, and ends later than the red group.
- Black curve: Starts at 'b', remains relatively flat near 'b', and ends latest.

Starling's law of the heart shows that cardiac output is always proportional to mean systemic filling pressure (the pressure of blood in the great veins). This is because the heart cannot suck blood through vessels (they collapse), it can only pressurise the blood which the great veins deliver to it.

Camels are adapted to withstand larger swings in osmolarity and core temperature than other mammals. Camels and humans both have the very rare ability to sweat. Sweat is mostly water, with a small amount of salt. (Note; camel humps are almost entirely fat, located to reduce surface area exposed to midday sun, similar to humans' unusually upright posture).

True or False?
Q.5.1 The change in blood osmolarity in the blue group is adaptive and helps them to last longer.
Q.5.2 The blue group drinks more water than the black group.
Q.5.3 Circulatory failure is the proximate cause of exhaustion in these conditions.
Q.5.4 Of the three groups, camels would follow a trajectory most similar to the blue group (but extended). Assume they do not eat or drink.
Q.5.5 A group given unlimited dry food, but not water, would last longer than the red group.

Part B
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also known as vasopressin) is usually released from the pituitary gland in proportion to blood osmolarity.
ADH acts on very-high affinity receptors in the kidney to increase urine concentration.
ADH also acts on low-affinity receptors across blood vessels, increasing their tone (squeezing on blood). Some patients have tumours which secrete ADH (syndromes of inappropriate ADH secretion).

True or False?
Q.5.6 These patients have more concentrated urine than normal.
Q.5.7 These patients have higher blood osmolarity than normal.
Q.5.8 In the absence of compensation, these patients have higher blood volume than normal.
Q.5.9 These patients have higher cardiac output than normal.
Q.5.10 These patients have similar fluid-handling problems to patients with uncontrolled diabetes.

Yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) prion protein Pma1 is found in two significantly different conformations.

In one of these conformations, the protein clumps resulting in loss of physiological function of the protein. This results in the [GAR+] phenotype. This phenotype is spread by cytoplasmic, non-Mendelian inheritance: sporadically daughter cells are formed which do not contain Pma1 protein clumps, so these have a [gar-] phenotype.

Catabolic repression describes the phenomenon of yeast using glucose as a sole source of carbon and energy, despite the presence of other organic compounds that yeast cells can use in metabolism. Only in the absence of glucose, will yeast cells use other sources of carbon and energy, e.g. glycerol.

In [GAR+] yeast, there is no catabolic repression.

Lactic acid secreted by *Staphylococcus gallinarum* bacteria, which live alongside *S. cerevisiae*, can induce a change in the yeast phenotype from [gar-] to [GAR+]. In an experiment, yeast was grown on solid agar-agar minimal medium containing glycerol (Gly) or glycerol plus glucosamine (Gly+GlcN). Glucosamine induces catabolic repression in yeast but is not metabolized by *S. cerevisiae*.

Figure 1 describes the results of this experiment in two panels, A and B.
Panel A shows the growth of cell suspensions on two solid agar minimal media: Gly + GlcN and Gly. The suspensions are serially diluted from right to left (indicated by X). The rows are labeled Y, F, C, D, and E, corresponding to the following treatments:
- Y: *S. cerevisiae* only (in duplicates). Result: Growth on Gly, no growth on Gly + GlcN.
- F: *S. cerevisiae* (in duplicates) plated adjacent to row C. Result: Growth on both Gly and Gly + GlcN.
- C: *S. gallinarum* (single row). Result: Growth on both Gly and Gly + GlcN.
- D: *S. cerevisiae* + filtered unused bacterial medium (in duplicates). Result: Growth on Gly, no growth on Gly + GlcN.
- E: *S. cerevisiae* + filtered medium after *S. gallinarum* cultivation (in duplicates). Result: Growth on both Gly and Gly + GlcN.

Panel B is a bar graph showing the relationship between lactic acid concentration (U, x-axis) and the fraction of [GAR+] colonies in the yeast population ± standard deviation (V, y-axis, logarithmic scale from 0.00001 to 1).
- At U = 0, V is approximately 0.0001.
- At U = 0.015625 to 0.25, V ranges from approximately 0.03 to 0.08.
- At U = 0.5, V is approximately 0.3.
- At U = 1, 2, and 4, V plateaus between approximately 0.7 and 0.8.

Indicate if each of the following statements is True or False.

Q. 10.1 A point mutation in the gene encoding the Pma1 protein, without any major conformational change, will result in the [GAR+] phenotype. (1.0 pt)

Q. 10.2 The occurrence of [gar-] cells is higher in cultures lacking lactic acid, than cultures containing lactic acid. (1.0 pt)

Q. 10.3 Cytoduction (the transfer of cytoplasm) from a [GAR+] cell to a [gar-] cell will change its phenotype to [GAR+]. (1.0 pt)

Q. 10.4 The results show that the biggest change in yeast phenotype is caused by the products of the bacteria themselves, rather than components of the bacterial medium. (1.0 pt)

Q. 10.5 Lactic acid secreted by *S. gallinarum* diffuses in the agar-agar solidified medium. (1.0 pt)

In an experiment, researchers designed a minimal genome similar to that of a bacteriophage, which encodes two proteins. When expressed in the host Escherichia coli, multiple copies of these proteins assemble into an icosahedral package and sometimes encapsulate the genetic material within.

Three variations were designed;
I53-50, which is known to assemble into an icosahedral structure,
I53-50-v1 which was a mutated sequence of I53-50 thus named version 1,
and the I53-50-Btat which was generated by genetically inserting a naturally occurring nucleic acid binding peptide (Btat) to the interior-facing terminus of the capsid.

To test for viability of these engineered "viruses" two experiments were performed. In the first experiment the host bacteria were lysed and debris was removed, then put through affinity and size exclusion chromatography. The resulting material was treated with RNAse and DNAse enzymes and visualized on gel electrophoresis stained for protein, nucleic acid, and nucleic acid after addition of reverse transcriptase.

B) after denaturation of the protein and addition of DNAse, nucleic acid content was examined. C) after denaturation of the proteins nucleic acid content was examined in the presence (shown by the plus sign above columns) and absence (shown by the minus sign above columns) of the reverse transcriptase (RT) enzyme. - Panel C (RT-PCR): Shows lanes for each variant with (+) and without (-) Reverse Transcriptase (RT). For I53-50, there are no bands in either + or - lanes. For v1, there is a strong band in the + lane and no band in the - lane. For Btat, there is a visible band in the + lane and no band in the - lane.]

In order to improve this capsid, a second experiment was performed. Researchers analyzed the effect of single site mutations on the enrichment of the genome; which shows the degree of protection provided by the capsid. By the end of this experiment, overall beneficial mutations were selected to produce I53-50-v2, or the version 2 of this capsid.

Figure 2. The second experiment was performed to improve the characteristics of the v1 nucleocapsids. The heat-map shows effects of various mutations on nucleic protection provided by the capsid. For the two proteins in the viral genome (denoted by the triangle and the pentagon), each column shows a site in the protein, and each row indicates what amino acid was substituted in that mutation. The effect of each of these mutations is represented as the color of that cell according to the color-bar. The text above each column shows the chosen mutation at that site at the end of the experiment. For example K179N indicates the starting sequence had a Lysine at the 179th site and was replaced by an Asparagine in the evolved capsid protein. This is also shown by the Blue squares and black dots which indicate the I53-50-v1 starting sequence and I53-50-v2 selected sequence, respectively.
[Image description for Figure 2: A heatmap showing the effects of various amino acid substitutions on the enrichment of the genome. The y-axis lists amino acids: K, R, D, E, N, Q, G. The color scale ranges from purple (Depleted, negative values down to -0.75) to white (neutral, 0) to orange (Enriched, positive values up to 0.75). Blue squares indicate the starting sequence (I53-50-v1), and black dots indicate the selected sequence (I53-50-v2). The row for amino acid K (Lysine) shows a mix of colors across different sites: some are orange (e.g., at E67K), some are white/grey, and some are purple (e.g., at E74D and E94E). The row for amino acid R (Arginine) also shows a mix of colors, including purple at some sites.]

True or False?
Q.11.1 The reason I53-50 did not package any nucleic acid is because it was unable to produce protein particles. (1.0pt)
Q.11.2 The genetic material packaged in the v1 and Btat variants is RNA. (1.0pt)

turns.question:
The basal metabolic rate of homoeothermic (warm-blooded) animals is described by Kleiber's law, which postulates that metabolic rate depends on animal mass according to a power law. The exponents vary between 2/3 (for relatively small size animals) and 3/4 (for relatively large animals).

Honey badgers are medium sized animals with a mass of about 6 kilograms. Assume the average daily consumed food energy honey badgers release is $2 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$.

Energy Consumption $= E = k \cdot m^\alpha$

Where $\alpha$ can be $2/3$ or $3/4$, $m$ is mass, and $k$ is a constant coefficient.

Q.16.1 Calculate the daily food energy consumption of a lesser jerboa with mass 60 grams. (Give your answer as an integer (whole number) in kJ).

Q.16.2 Calculate the daily food energy consumption of a camel with mass 600 kilograms. (Give your answer in MJ to 1 decimal point).

Q.16.3 Calculate how many lesser jerboas could feed on the desert area sufficient for one camel feeding.

Give your answer as an integer (whole number).

Q.16.1: 3 points for an answer in the range 93-94.
Q.16.2: 3 points for an answer in the range 63.0-63.5.
Q.16.3: 3 points for an answer in the range 670-685.

Total: 9 points.

turns.question:
Defending a territory requires time and energy. Any animal should only defend territories if the benefits of defence outweigh the costs.

Consider a bird species that feeds only on the nectar of flowers. The table below shows the foraging time required for the bird to meet its daily energy requirements when it obtains given amounts of nectar per flower.

The metabolic costs associated with various activities of the bird are as follows:
- Foraging for nectar: 500 calories/h
- Sitting on a perch: 200 calories/h
- Territory defence: 1500 calories/h

| Nectar per flower (microlitres) | Time to get energy (hours) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 8 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 2.7 |

If a bird defends a territory, it excludes other nectar consumers and this increases the amount of nectar per flower from 2 microlitres to 3 microlitres. The bird thus spends less time foraging and more time sitting on a perch.

Answer the following questions:

Q. 19.1 Calculate the energy saved by this bird, with reduced foraging time, as compared to an individual, which is not territorial. (in calories)

Q. 19.2 If the bird needs to spend 0.28 hours per day defending territory, instead of perching, what is the cost of defence faced by the bird, compared to a bird which is not territorial? (in calories)

True or False?
Q. 19.3.1 Under the conditions specified above, the bird is likely to show territorial defence.
Q. 19.3.2 The birds will almost never be territorial if it reduces the amount of time spent perching.
Q. 19.3.3 The birds will almost always be territorial if the cost of foraging per hour is higher than the cost of defence per hour.
Q. 19.3.4 The birds will not show territorial defence when the net costs, incurred by defence, are lower than those of not defending a territory.

The pied flycatcher (Ficedula hypoleuca) and collared flycatcher (F. albicollis) are two closely related and morphologically very similar bird species.

Their cross-species hybrids are completely sterile.

Their geographical distributions partially overlap.

A recent study recorded songs of 168 male flycatchers of both species from different geographic locations. Various acoustic parameters of individual songs were measured, and differences between songs were visualized using principal component analysis (PCA). PCA integrates different parameters of the song and transforms them into principal components (PC), which allows for the reduction of multidimensional data to a few dimensions (two in this case, PC1 and PC2). Similar songs will have similar values for a given principal component.

The recorded songs were also played to F. hypoleuca nestlings and the nestlings' begging calls in response to the songs were counted.

In this study, the rate at which nestlings responded to the played male songs from their population did not correlate with how similar the played songs were to the songs of their social fathers. Social fathers are the male whose calls nestlings hear most often.

**Figure 1A & 1B Descriptions:**
Figure 1A shows the geographic distribution of F. hypoleuca (yellow) and F. albicollis (blue) and their overlap (green). Colored dots show F. hypoleuca populations used in the study, which are distributed across both allopatric and sympatric regions.
Figure 1B shows the results of Principal Components Analysis. Each dot corresponds to a single individual's song. Blue and yellow ellipses include 95% of the data points of the corresponding species. The yellow ellipse (F. hypoleuca) and blue ellipse (F. albicollis) are completely separated along the PC1 axis. Within the yellow ellipse, dots of the same color (representing the same F. hypoleuca population from Figure 1A) tend to cluster together.

**Figure 2 Description:**
Figure 2 shows the number of begging calls (N) by F. hypoleuca nestlings (mean per clutch) in response to a recorded song of F. hypoleuca (yellow) or F. albicollis (blue) males.
- Group X (Allopatry: 6 populations, 347 clutches): Nestlings responded with significantly more begging calls to F. hypoleuca songs than to F. albicollis songs (P < 0.001).
- Group Y (Sympatry: 1 population, 37 clutches): There was no significant difference in the number of begging calls in response to F. hypoleuca songs versus F. albicollis songs (P = 0.136).

**Figure 3 Description:**
Figure 3 shows the number of begging calls (N) by F. hypoleuca nestlings (mean per clutch) in response to recorded F. hypoleuca songs which are:
- LS (Local-similar, grey): similar to songs of the nestlings' local population.
- LD (Local-dissimilar, black): dissimilar to songs of the nestlings' local population.
- CS (Collared-similar, blue): similar to songs of F. albicollis.
The results show that the response to LS is significantly higher than to LD (P = 0.035). The response to LD is not significantly different from the response to CS (P = 0.999).

True or False?

Q.20.1 These results support the existence of local song dialects in F. hypoleuca. 1.0pt

Q.20.2 These results support the idea that song differences between F. hypoleuca and F. albicollis evolved primarily as an adaptation to avoid cross-species hybridization. 1.0pt

Q.20.3 This study provides evidence that F. hypoleuca nestlings learn their songs from their social fathers. 1.0pt

Q.20.4 It might be expected that genome-average genetic differences between F. hypoleuca populations will increase over time. 1.0pt

turns.question:
Gregor Mendel described the inheritance of round and wrinkled pea seeds. He showed the round (R) phenotype was dominant over wrinkled (r).

After 135 years, the gene SBE1, and the insertion of a transposable element, which caused the wrinkled phenotype, were discovered. SBE1 codes for an enzyme involved in starch biosynthesis. Wrinkled seeds are characterized by higher levels of sucrose, and lower levels of starch, compared to round seeds.

In a PCR test, a pair of primers, targeting flanking sides of the site of insertion, are used to amplify the genomic DNA. The products are resolved by agarose gel electrophoresis.

A geneticist made two independent crosses (I and II) between peas with different genotypes. 30 progeny from each cross was analyzed by PCR. Each lane in the gel below represents analysis of one progeny.

[Gel Electrophoresis Results Description]
The results show two agarose gels, labeled I and II, each with 30 lanes representing 30 progeny from Cross I and Cross II respectively. The downward arrow denotes the direction of migration (smaller fragments migrate further down).
In both gels, bands appear at two distinct positions: an upper position (slower migration, larger fragment) and a lower position (faster migration, smaller fragment).
- In Gel I: The upper band is present in all lanes except lanes 6, 12, 18, 24, and 30. The lower band is present in all lanes except lanes 3, 9, 15, 21, and 27. Thus, lanes 3, 9, 15, 21, and 27 have only the upper band; lanes 6, 12, 18, 24, and 30 have only the lower band; and all other lanes have both bands.
- In Gel II: The upper band is present in all 30 lanes. The lower band is present in odd-numbered lanes (1, 3, 5, etc.) and absent in even-numbered lanes (2, 4, 6, etc.). Thus, odd-numbered lanes have both bands, and even-numbered lanes have only the upper band.

Q.22.1 Identify the parents for each of the cross by choosing the appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) (2.0pt):
(A) Rr × RR
(B) rr × Rr
(C) Rr × Rr
(D) rr × RR

Q.22.1.1 Cross I
Q.22.1.2 Cross II

Q.22.2 In cross I, what kind of seeds does individual 3 produce when self-pollinated? (1.0pt)
A. Round
B. Wrinkled
C. A mixture of round and wrinkled seeds
D. All seeds are semi-wrinkled.

Q.22.3 True or false? (1.0pt)
Heterozygous seeds have higher levels of SBE1 activity compared to insertion homozygotes. (Answer T or F)

turns.question:
Identifying genetic relatedness between human individuals is useful for many applications.

A common approach to this is based on detecting identical-by-descent (IBD) segments shared by two individuals. IBD segments are chromosomal segments that the two individuals inherited from a common ancestor, and hence are identical in sequence except for any mutations that happened since that common ancestor. IBD segment ends correspond to sites where recombination happened.

At a given position in the genome two individuals can share 0, 1 or 2 IBD segments (IBD0, IBD1 and IBD2 states respectively). Looking at the fraction of the genome in IBD1 and IBD2 states, for a given pair of individuals, is a common practice to infer genealogical relationships between individuals.

In questions 24.1, 24.2 and 24.3 assume that parents of any individual are completely unrelated and don't share any IBD segments.

Indicate the expected fraction of the genome (in percentage, with 100 being the maximum) in IBD1 and IBD2 states between pairs of individuals with the family relationship listed below.

1. Monozygotic twins
2. Parent-offspring
3. Full-siblings
4. Half-siblings
5. Grandparent-grandchild

Q24.1 Fraction of the genome IBD1 state.
Provide the IBD1 fraction (%) for relationships 1 to 5.

Q24.2 Fraction of the genome IBD2 state.
Provide the IBD2 fraction (%) for relationships 1 to 5.

Q24.3 Choose the relationship types for which notable biological variation in IBD sharing is expected. Indicate types which show variation as True, and others as False.
Provide True or False for relationships 1 to 5.

Q24.4 True or False?
Q24.4.1 On average, IBD segments shared between a parent and an offspring are longer compared to those shared between full siblings.
Q24.4.2 If we trace one's family tree deep into the past, in the 30th generation we will find $2^{30}$ people this individual shares IBD with.
Q24.4.3 The fraction of IBD1 genome between two randomly picked individuals from a single population is higher in populations with smaller effective population size.

The average pairwise difference between a pair of sequences in a population is called nucleotide diversity, which is a simple measure of the genetic diversity of a population.

Figure 1 describes 3 alleles (A, B, C) in terms of their frequency in a given population (Column 2). Column 3 provides the nucleotide sequences: for alleles B and C only the sequence differences from allele A are provided while positions with the same nucleotide as in A are marked with an asterisk "*".

Figure 1:
Allele | Frequency | Sequence
A | 0.5 | GTATAGACTAGATCTACATGTAGCTGACTGCATATGCTGT
B | 0.3 | ****T********A*******G***A**************
C | 0.2 | *********C**********A*******************

Nucleotide diversity can be calculated using the following formula:

$\pi = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (f_i \times f_j \times d_{ij})$

- Where $\pi$ is nucleotide diversity,
- $n$ is the total number of alleles,
- $f_i$ and $f_j$ are frequencies of two alleles,
- $d_{ij}$ is the difference between the two alleles. For example, sequences A and B differ by 4 bases out of 40, so the difference between them is 0.1.

Q.25.1 Calculate the nucleotide diversity in this population. Give the correct answer to 3 decimal places. (3.0 pt)

Q.25.2 Cheetahs were found to have significantly lower genome-wide genetic diversity than other mammals. Select the likeliest explanation for this observation: (1.0 pt)
A. Cheetahs adapted very rapidly to the environment.
B. Cheetahs have an extremely high mutation rate.
C. The population of cheetahs went through a bottleneck in the recent past.
D. Natural selection is extremely efficient in removing mutations from Cheetahs' gene pool.

Figure 2 plots nucleotide diversity (y-axis, ranging from 0.0 to 0.05), in 300 bp sliding windows along the sequence of gene Y (x-axis), for a modern cultivated crop plant (dashed line 2) and its wild ancestor (solid line 1). Below the plot the structure of the gene is shown: boxes indicate exons, with grey areas being protein-coding regions and white areas being untranslated regions. The thin bent line shows the intron; the 5' end is on the left.

Figure 2 Description:
Aligned below the x-axis is the structure of gene Y, from 5' (left) to 3' (right):
- Upstream region
- Box B: Exon 1 (contains a short white untranslated area followed by a grey protein-coding area)
- Region A: Intron (shown as a thin bent line)
- Box C: Exon 2 (grey protein-coding area followed by a white untranslated area)
- Downstream region

Data trends from the plot:
- Upstream of Exon 1: The wild ancestor (line 1) has high nucleotide diversity (fluctuating between ~0.02 and 0.05). The cultivated crop (line 2) has very low nucleotide diversity (~0.0).
- Exon 1, Intron, Exon 2, and Downstream: The nucleotide diversity of both the wild ancestor (line 1) and the cultivated crop (line 2) are nearly identical. Both drop to low levels (~0.01) through Exon 1, the Intron, and most of Exon 2, and then both rise together to ~0.03 at the 3' end of Exon 2 and downstream.

It has been concluded from the results in Figure 2 that a mutation in this locus was positively selected during the domestication process.

Q.25.3 What is the most likely effect of this mutation? (1.0 pt)
A. It results in an amino acid substitution in the encoded protein.
B. It affects splicing of gene Y.
C. It affects expression of gene Y.
D. It results in a premature stop codon in gene Y.

True or false?
Q.25.4.1 This data suggests purifying selection is acting more strongly on this locus in the wild ancestor than in the domesticated crop. (1.0 pt)
Q.25.4.2 This data suggests, that in the wild ancestor, purifying selection is acting more strongly on the sequence upstream of exon 1 compared to the intron of gene Y. (1.0 pt)
Q.25.4.3 No recombination occurred in the analysed region during the domestication process. (1.0 pt)

turns.question:
The question involves two transgenic plant lines, P1 and P2, that produce bisexual flowers.

P1 is transformed with barnase gene linked to a gene (HR) conferring resistance to a herbicide.

Expression of the Barnase protein in this plant inhibits pollen formation making the plant unable to produce fertile pollen. Male sterility and herbicide resistance are both dominant characters.

P2 is transformed with barstar gene, also linked to the HR gene. In the presence of Barstar protein the activity of Barnase protein is inhibited, restoring pollen formation. The activity of the Barstar protein is a dominant character.

In P1, the barnase gene lies in linkage group 2, whilst in P2, the barstar gene is in linkage group 3.

P1 is hemizygous for the barnase and HR genes. P2 is homozygous for both the barstar and HR genes.

A cross is made between P1 and P2. The F1 progeny are self-pollinated and the F2 progeny are analyzed.

Q. 26.1 What percentage of F1 progeny will be unable to produce fertile pollen?
Q. 26.2 What percentage of F1 progeny will be herbicide resistant?
Q. 26.3 What percentage of F2 progeny will be unable to produce fertile pollen? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
Q. 26.4 What percentage of F2 progeny will be herbicide resistant? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

Since the loci are unlinked (different chromosomes), the gamete can have any combination of the two independent segregation decisions. However there is the issue of linkage: Genes within each chromosome stay together, but across chromosomes they assort independently.

Thus the possible gametes from a given parent are each combination of LG2 allele (T2 or N2) and LG3 allele (T3 or N3), yielding 2x2=4 possible haplotypes.

Their frequencies depend on parent's genotype at each locus. For each F1 genotype, genotype at LG2 and LG3 can be either heterozygous (one T, one N) or homozygous (N/N) etc. We'll compute for each case.

Case A: Genotype: LG2 = T2/N2 (heterozygous), LG3 = T3/N3 (heterozygous). Thus each locus segregates 1/2 for T, 1/2 for N. Since they assort independently, the gamete haplotype frequencies: each of the four combos have probability (1/2)*(1/2)=1/4.

Thus gamete types from Case A: T2 T3 (1/4); T2 N3 (1/4); N2 T3 (1/4); N2 N3 (1/4).

Since the parent is hermaphroditic (bisexual flowers), but with selfing, the same pool is used for both male and female gametes. So the cross is essentially a dihybrid cross where the gamete frequencies are as above. The resulting F2 genotype frequencies can be computed by taking pairwise combination of gametes: genotype probabilities = sum_{i,j} p_i * p_j (if self-fertilized) where i,j are gamete types (including same type twice). For a self cross of a heterozygous individual, the genotype frequencies follow standard ratios (9:3:3:1) if both loci are heterozygous. But here we have a mixture of cases, and the gamete distribution may differ.

We need to compute the overall percentage of F2 that are male sterile (unable to produce fertile pollen) i.e., genotype: barnase present (T2 allele) and barstar absent (N3/N3). Actually sterility occurs when at least one T2 allele present (B+) AND both chromosomes lack T3 (i.e., N3/N3). Because if you have only one copy of T2 (any), and N3/N3, you're sterile. Similarly if you have T2 present in heterozygous state (T2/N2) and N3/N3, you are sterile. Also if you have T2/T2 (both copies) and N3/N3, still sterile. So genotype for sterility: presence of at least one T2 allele, and zero copies of T3. Equivalent to genotype where at LG2 allele count T2 >= 1, and at LG3 allele count T3 = 0 (i.e., N3/N3). Thus to compute proportion of F2 sterile, we need to sum probabilities of genotype categories satisfying those conditions across the overall F2 distribution.

1. Compute probability of each F1 genotype: 0.5 case A, 0.5 case B.

2. For each F1 genotype, compute the gamete distribution and then the self-cross genotype probabilities. Then weight each resulting genotype proportion by the probability of that F1 genotype (0.5) to get overall contributions to F2.

3. Sum contributions to get overall fractions for sterile and resistant.

Given the symmetry and small number of possibilities, we can compute directly.

- Type 1: (T2,T3) - call g1
- Type 2: (T2,N3) - g2
- Type 3: (N2,T3) - g3
- Type 4: (N2,N3) - g4

P(g2) = 0.5 * 1/4 = 1/8 = 0.125

P(g4) = 0.5 * 1/4 + 0.5 * 0.5 = 1/8 + 0.25 = 0.375

g2: 12.5%
g3: 37.5%
g4: 37.5%

turns.question:
When eukaryotic nuclear genes are being actively transcribed, their chromatin is usually more relaxed. This leaves the underlying DNA more sensitive to the enzymatic activity of DNase I.

Chromatin was purified from each of pancreatic islet of Langerhans cells, hepatocytes, spermatids and skeletal muscle cells. The chromatin was then exposed to progressively increasing concentrations of DNase I, followed by DNA purification and digestion with restriction endonucleases.

The resulting DNA fragments were subjected to electrophoresis, denaturation and Southern hybridization (with radiolabeled ssDNA probes complementary to the histone, insulin, acetylcholine receptor or actin gene).

Restriction fragments of a particular length correspond to particular genes:
- 2.5 kb = histone H2A
- 3.0 kb = insulin
- 3.3 kb = acetylcholine receptor
- 4.0 kb = actin

The autoradiograms (A-D) show the results for each cell type. The x-axis denotes DNase I concentration in $\mu g/ml$ (0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0). A band that fades and disappears at higher DNase I concentrations indicates that the gene is sensitive to DNase I. A band that persists across all concentrations indicates that the gene is resistant to DNase I.

Based on the autoradiograms, the sensitivity of the fragments is as follows:
- Autoradiogram A: The 4.0 kb and 2.5 kb bands are sensitive to DNase I. The 3.3 kb and 3.0 kb bands are resistant.
- Autoradiogram B: The 4.0 kb, 3.0 kb, and 2.5 kb bands are sensitive to DNase I. The 3.3 kb band is resistant.
- Autoradiogram C: The 4.0 kb, 3.3 kb, and 2.5 kb bands are sensitive to DNase I. The 3.0 kb band is resistant.
- Autoradiogram D: Only the 4.0 kb band is sensitive to DNase I. The 3.3 kb, 3.0 kb, and 2.5 kb bands are resistant.

Match the autoradiograms A-D with the corresponding cell types:
1. Pancreatic $\beta$ cells
2. Hepatocytes
3. Spermatids
4. Skeletal muscle cells

Provide your answer as a sequence of four letters (A, B, C, or D) corresponding to cell types 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively, separated by spaces.

Brain microglia (a type of macrophage) perform many roles in the central nervous system.

The role of microglia in synaptic reorganisation and circuit rewiring, which modulates memory, was tested in mice. Mice were trained to freeze when receiving a stimulus (Figure A). The % of mice remembering to freeze 5 days, and 35 days, after training is shown in Figure B.

The % of mice remembering to freeze 35 days after training were compared with Pexidartinib (PLX) and without (PLX) treatment at the start of the study (shown in Figure D). Pexidartinib (PLX) selectively removes only microglial cells. A single Pexidartinib treatment permanently removes microglial cells.

**Figure A and B Description:**
Figure A shows the experimental design. Mice undergo Training (a) and are tested (c) after 5 days (b). Another group undergoes Training (d) and is tested (f) after 35 days (e).
Figure B is a bar chart showing Freezing (%) (Y) on the y-axis. The freezing percentage for the 5-day group (b) is approximately 72%, and for the 35-day group (e) is approximately 21%. The difference is statistically significant (****).

**Figure C and D Description:**
Figure C shows the experimental design for the PLX treatment. Mice undergo Training (g) and are tested (k) after 35 days (h). During this period, they receive either Control (i) or PLX (j) treatment.
Figure D is a bar chart showing Freezing (%) (Y) on the y-axis. The freezing percentage for the Control group (i) is approximately 28%, and for the PLX group (j) is approximately 50%. The difference is statistically significant (**).

Indicate whether each of the following statements is True or False (1.0 pt each):
Q.9.1 Forgetting is an active process involving microglial cells.
Q.9.2 The microglial population is usually self-renewing, rather than replaced by bone-marrow cells.
Q.9.3 Depletion of the microglia in the brain leads to an enhanced ability to forget the behavioural response.
Q.9.4 Given that the result in (D) could be mimicked by the application of an inhibitor of phagocytosis; the potential mechanism explaining the results is physical removal of the synapse by microglial phagocytosis.

Cold-blooded (poikilothermic) animals are able to tolerate significant fluctuations in body temperature (by several tens of degrees) without negative consequences.

In contrast, some warm-blooded (homoiothermic) animals cannot survive a small change in body temperature (see Table).

| Group of animals | Normal core body temperature, °C | Lethal core body temperature, °C |
|---|---|---|
| Monotremata (Echidna) | 30-31 | 37 |
| Marsupials | 35-36 | 40-41 |
| Insectivores (Hedgehog) | 34-36 | 41 |
| Human | 37 | 43 |
| Most of placental mammals | 36-38 | 42-44 |
| Birds (Kiwi) | 38 | 44 |
| Birds (except Passerines) | 39-40 | 46 |

Indicate whether each of the following statements is True or False:

13.1 For Passerines birds (body temperature is 40 - 41 °C) lethal core body temperature will be about 47 °C.

What is/are the main reason(s) warm-blooded animals are intolerant to changes in body temperature? State whether the following statements are true or false:

13.2 Thermal denaturation of the majority of enzymes and other proteins with increasing temperature.
13.3 Thermal denaturation (melting) of DNA with increasing temperature.
13.4 Changes in the microviscosity of lipids of cellular and intracellular membranes with increasing temperature.
13.5 Different temperature sensitivity (Q10-coefficient) of biochemical reactions in cells.

13.2: False (1 point)

13.5: True (1 point)
Total: 5 points.

5'- N N N [G G T C T C] N | N N N N N N N -3'
3'- N N N [C C A G A G] N N N N N | N N -5'

...TAAGCGAGACC_ X _GGTCTCTATACC...

ATCGGTCTCTGTAT_ $\overrightarrow{y1}$ _ATACCGAGACCGCA

ATCGGTCTCTTAAG_ $\overrightarrow{y2}$ _GTATCGAGACCGCA

y1: Insert 1
y2: Insert 2

a) $\overrightarrow{y1}$ $\overrightarrow{y2}$
b) $\overrightarrow{y2}$ $\overrightarrow{y1}$
c) $\overleftarrow{y2}$ $\overleftarrow{y1}$

During Agrobacterium-mediated transformation of plants, one or more copies of T-DNA (Transfer DNA) can integrate randomly into the plant genomic DNA.

The number of T-DNA insertions can be analyzed by Southern hybridization of digested genomic DNA from transformed plants, using probes against sequences within the T-DNA.

The restriction enzyme used for digestion of genomic DNA should preferably have a single cut site within the T-DNA. The restriction enzyme would cut within the integrated T-DNA, and also in the flanking genomic DNA.

Figure 1 represents a circular vector (15 Kb) used for plant transformation. The T-DNA region (5 Kb) lies between the LB (left border) and RB (right border).
The elements within the T-DNA, ordered from LB to RB, are:
- Probe A region
- Restriction site X
- Restriction site Y
- Probe B region
Outside the T-DNA, in the vector backbone, there is another restriction site for enzyme Y.
There are no other X or Y sites shown on the vector.

Figure 2 represents the results of Southern hybridization carried out with DNA from independently transformed plants (1 to 5) and DNA from an untransformed plant (UT). Hybridization was carried out with either probe A or B.
The blot for Probe A shows the following number of bands for each lane:
- UT: 0 bands
- Plant 1: 2 bands
- Plant 2: 1 band
- Plant 3: 2 bands
- Plant 4: 0 bands
- Plant 5: 4 bands
The blot for Probe B shows the following number of bands for each lane:
- UT: 0 bands
- Plant 1: 1 band
- Plant 2: 1 band
- Plant 3: 2 bands
- Plant 4: 1 band
- Plant 5: 3 bands
The bands across the different plants appear at various different positions, indicating variable fragment lengths.

Determine if each of the following statements is True (T) or False (F). Output your answer as a space-separated sequence of T and F.

Q.26.1 The genomic DNA was digested with restriction enzyme Y.
Q.26.2 The digested DNA fragments that hybridized to the probe contain regions of T-DNA only.
Q.26.3 There are two copies of T-DNA in plant number 1.
Q.26.4 One copy of T-DNA is integrated in plant number 2.
Q.26.5 Complete T-DNA region has been transferred in plant 4.

turns.question:
Imagine you need to sequence DNA from a 25,000-year-old bone specimen.

For this, DNA can be isolated using the following steps:
1. Grind the bone into powder in liquid nitrogen.
2. Add buffer with high salt concentration (high-salt buffer; HSB) to the powder and incubate.
3. Add silica particles to the powder suspension and incubate.
4. Remove the silica particles from the HSB and wash them with fresh HSB.
5. Elute DNA from the silica particles using a buffer with low salt concentration.

This DNA isolation method is based on the ability of DNA to bind to silica particles in HSB as shown in Figure 1B.

[Figure 1 description:
Panel A shows the chemical structures of five nitrogenous bases labeled C (Cytosine), T (Thymine), U (Uracil), A (Adenine), and G (Guanine).
Panel B illustrates the principles of DNA purification on a silica sorbent. It shows a DNA double helix above a silica surface with exposed Si-O⁻ groups. 
- Initially, water molecules interact with the Si-O⁻ groups. 
- After the addition of NaCl (+NaCl), Na⁺ ions form a bridge between the DNA double helix and the negatively charged O⁻ atoms on the silica surface (Si-O⁻). 
- After the removal of NaCl (-NaCl), the DNA is released, and water molecules again interact with the silica surface.]

Evaluate the following statements as True or False:

Q.28.1 This DNA isolation method could also be used for modern samples.
Q.28.2 This DNA isolation method allows scientists to obtain intact (full-length) chromosomes.
Q.28.3 The DNA sample obtained with this method could be contaminated with bacterial DNA.
Q.28.4 DNA binds to the silica particles via positively charged nitrogenous bases.
Q.28.5 As some DNA bases undergo deamination when exposed to the environment, ancient DNA will contain more uracil compared to modern DNA of the same species.

question_images.description: Figure 1 consists of two panels. Panel A shows the chemical structures of five nitrogenous bases: Cytosine (C), Thymine (T), Uracil (U), Adenine (A), and Guanine (G). Panel B illustrates the principles of DNA purification on a silica sorbent. It shows a DNA double helix above a silica surface with exposed Si-O⁻ groups. Initially, water molecules (shown with partial charges δ⁺ on H and δ⁻ on O) interact with the Si-O⁻ groups. After the addition of NaCl (+NaCl), Na⁺ ions form a bridge between the DNA double helix and the negatively charged O⁻ atoms on the silica surface (Si-O⁻). After the removal of NaCl (-NaCl), the DNA is released, and water molecules again interact with the silica surface.

Researchers conducted a study to determine if parasite-mediated competition was occurring in squirrels. Four species of squirrel were trapped, and the presence of parasite eggs was determined.

Cryptic species are organisms that look identical, but which represent distinct evolutionary lineages.

The diversity and geographical distribution of two cryptic species of Aricia butterflies, A. agestis and A. cramera, were studied.

[Figure Description: A phylogenetic tree of four Aricia species alongside maps of their geographical distribution in Europe and North Africa.
Phylogenetic tree topology:
- The root splits into A. cramera (IV) and a clade containing the other three species.
- This clade splits into A. agestis (I) and a sub-clade containing A. artaxerxes (II) and A. montensis (III).
Geographical distributions:
- I - A. agestis: Widespread across central, eastern, and southern Europe, but absent from the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa.
- II - A. artaxerxes: Patchy distribution in northern Europe and some central European mountain ranges.
- III - A. montensis: Restricted mainly to the Iberian Peninsula.
- IV - A. cramera: Widespread in the Iberian Peninsula, North Africa, and some Mediterranean islands.

| Species | Elevation | Host Plants |
|---|---|---|
| A. agestis | 0-1700 m | Erodium, Geranium, Helianthemum |
| A. artaxerxes | 0-2200 m | Erodium, Geranium, Helianthemum |
| A. montensis | 1000-2800 m | Erodium, Helianthemum |
| A. cramera | 0-2800 m | Erodium, Geranium, Helianthemum |

Determine if the following statements are True or False:

Q.31.1 The pair of studied cryptic species apparently formed because of geographical isolation.
Q.31.2 These cryptic species have a clear ecological confinement to certain habitats.
Q.31.3 Aricia species without an exact specialization can coexist with species that are clearly confined to a limited range of habitats.
Q.31.4 Specialist Aricia species could be formed from generalist ancestors with wide geographical areas of distribution.

Seabirds spend much of their lives in the open ocean foraging but, during breeding, they congregate on remote islands or cliffs to nest. **Figure Descriptions:**
**Figure A** is a map showing the foraging distribution of the four seabird species. The map shows landmasses (grey) along the western and southern edges.

- Razorbill (Blue) foraging areas are scattered, with many patches located near the western and southern coastlines.
- Common Murre (Orange) foraging areas are scattered centrally and southerly.
- Thick-billed Murre (Pink) foraging areas are concentrated in the northern and eastern offshore regions.

|---|---|

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colour code | Black | Blue | Orange | Pink |
| Maximum diving depth (meters) | 60 | 120 | 180+ | 180+ |

Based on the figures above, state if the following statements are true or false.

Q.32.1 The foraging patterns indicate evidence of niche segregation in Atlantic Puffins and Razorbills. (1.0pt)
Q.32.2 Common Murres and Thick-billed Murres have similar diets. (1.0pt)

Corals form mutualistic associations with a dinoflagellate, Symbiodinium of the family Symbiodiniaceae. Symbiodinium has two major life stages: a flagellated stage, called mastigote, and an aflagellated stage, called coccoid.

When Symbiodinium is grown in culture, each coccoid cell undergoes cell division to produce two mastigote cells. The mastigotes swim for a few days before they shed their flagella and metamorphose into the coccoid stage.

However, within the host coral cells, there is a dramatic change in Symbiodinium life history, with a marked reduction in cell proliferation and a severe reduction in the number of mastigotes. It is assumed that the coral host regulates the metamorphosis of Symbiodinium, and evidence suggests that certain nutrients may serve as limiting factors.

In an experiment, Symbiodinium microadriaticum cells were cultured outside their host cells, under nutrient-limited free-living conditions, to determine the importance of different nutrients for regulating cell proliferation and differentiation.

Figure A shows cell proliferation curves of S. microadriaticum from Days 6 to 16, after subculturing in free-living conditions, with the selective depletion of the indicated nutrients. The error bars represent standard errors of the mean.
Approximate data for Figure A (Y-axis is 10^5 Cells / ml, X-axis is Days):
- Day 6: Control ~1.4, Nitrogen depleted ~0.6, Iron depleted ~0.5, Phosphate depleted ~0.4
- Day 8: Control ~2.0, Nitrogen depleted ~0.8, Iron depleted ~0.7, Phosphate depleted ~0.6
- Day 10: Control ~3.2, Nitrogen depleted ~1.6, Iron depleted ~1.7, Phosphate depleted ~1.2
- Day 12: Control ~3.8, Nitrogen depleted ~2.7, Iron depleted ~1.8, Phosphate depleted ~2.4
- Day 14: Control ~5.4, Nitrogen depleted ~4.0, Iron depleted ~2.1, Phosphate depleted ~3.0
- Day 16: Control ~6.2, Nitrogen depleted ~4.1, Iron depleted ~2.6, Phosphate depleted ~3.5

Figure B shows the relative proportions of mastigotes and coccoid cells of S. microadriaticum (one replicate culture per column, three replicates per condition), again under free-living conditions, with the depletion of the indicated nutrients.
Approximate data for Figure B (% Mastigote / % Coccoid):
- Control: Rep 1 (~68% / 32%), Rep 2 (~68% / 32%), Rep 3 (~73% / 27%)
- Nitrogen depleted: Rep 1 (~35% / 65%), Rep 2 (~40% / 60%), Rep 3 (~30% / 70%)
- Iron depleted: Rep 1 (~82% / 18%), Rep 2 (~85% / 15%), Rep 3 (~90% / 10%)
- Phosphate depleted: Rep 1 (~63% / 37%), Rep 2 (~71% / 29%), Rep 3 (~75% / 25%)

## True or False?

Q.33.1 All three nutrients tested affected the mean values of both proliferation and differentiation of S. microadriaticum cells.

Q. 33.2 Nitrogen was the only limiting nutrient for the differentiation of S. microadriaticum cells within host coral cells.

Q. 33.3 Given the above data, it is possible that the changing coccoid / mastigote ratios in the cultures are a side effect of the marked reduction in cell proliferation.

Q. 33.4 Phosphate had relatively the greatest restrictive effect on cell proliferation over the experimental period.

Q.33.5 These results suggest that it may be possible for coral host cells to increase the levels of certain nutrients to regulate the differentiation of S. microadriaticum cells.

Q.34.4 The male-to-female ratio of subadults reflects the male-to-female ratio of juveniles in this population in subsequent years.

Now process the following competition-level biology question:

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis consists of:

1. amplification of a DNA fragment by PCR,

2. digestion of the PCR product with a restriction enzyme,

3. DNA electrophoresis.

The RFLP method was used to detect the recessive allele of the GNPTAB gene, which causes a genetic disease in cats - mucolipidosis II. A point mutation in the recessive allele changes the sequence of the 882nd codon of the gene from CAG to TAG.

The diagram shows the result of analysis the GNPTAB gene of related cats. A 414 bp fragment of the GNPTAB gene was amplified and digested with the restriction enzyme PstI. Pstl recognises and cuts the sequence: 5'-CTGCAG-3'.

Part A presents the family tree, while part B presents the result of the RFLP analysis. The analysis was also performed using the genetic material of an unrelated healthy cat (designated as "Normal"). There was another sample which contained water during PCR, instead of template DNA (designated as "H2O").

**Part A: Pedigree**
- Individual 3739 (male, not studied) is the father of two females (both not studied).
- The first female (not studied) mated with a male (not studied) to produce a son, 4977 (male, healthy).
- The second female (not studied) mated with a male (not studied) to produce a daughter, 6431 (female, healthy).
- 4977 and 6431 mated and produced five offspring:
  - 7160 (female, affected)
  - 7161 (male, healthy)
  - 7162 (male, affected)
  - 7163 (male, affected)
  - 7164 (male, healthy)

**Part B: RFLP Analysis (Gel Electrophoresis)**
The gel shows the following bands for each lane:
- Lane M (Marker): Bands at 500, 400, 300, and 200 bp.
- Lane 4977: Bands at 414, 231, and 183 bp.
- Lane 7160: Band at 414 bp.
- Lane 7161: Bands at 231 and 183 bp.
- Lane 7162: Band at 414 bp.
- Lane 7163: Band at 414 bp.
- Lane 7164: Bands at 414, 231, and 183 bp.
- Lane 6431: Bands at 414, 231, and 183 bp.
- Lane N (Normal): Bands at 231 and 183 bp.
- Lane H2O: No bands.

True or false?

Q. 41.1 The recessive allele of GNPTAB gene makes the encoded protein shorter. 1.0pt

Q. 41.2 The 414 bp-long DNA fragment corresponds to the recessive allele of GNPTAB gene. 1.0pt

Q. 41.3 Mucolipidosis II in cats is inherited as X-linked recessive disease. 1.0pt

Q. 41.4 Cat number 3739 must be homozygous for the recessive allele of GNPTAB gene. 1.0pt

As more and more human genomes are being sequenced, storing this information has become an issue.

One way to reduce the size of the files containing sequence data is to store only the information about the differences between the sequenced genomes and a "reference genome". (The reference genome is haploid).

Such file format is called Variant Call Format (vcf), and is in essence a table like the one below. In this example there is information about the genomes of 2 individuals, but any number of genomes (from 1 to many thousands) can be stored in one file.

| Chromosome | Position | Reference allele | Alternative alleles | Genotypes Individual 1 | Genotypes Individual 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5897 | G | A | 0/1 | 0/0 |
| 1 | 6908 | C | T | 0/0 | 1/1 |
| 1 | 7100 | A | C, T | 0/2 | 1/2 |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

In the columns "Genotypes" 0 stands for the nucleotide being the same as the reference allele, while other numbers stand for the nucleotide being the same as alternative alleles in the order they appear in the "Alternative alleles" column.

Note, In this question ONLY consider single nucleotide variants (SNVs, SNPs, switches of a single base) and consider the genomes of all people to be exactly equal length.

## True or false?

Q.42.1 Individual 1 from the example above is homozygous at the position 7100 on chromosome 1. (1.0 pt)

The 2022 Nobel Prize was awarded for sequencing ancient DNA to study the human past.

This work produced whole genomes of several Neanderthals and one Denisovan (another group of archaic hominins).

The figure depicts trees showing phylogenetic relationships between those archaic specimens and different groups of modern humans.

Figure 1. Cladograms based on mitochondrial DNA sequence (a), and average genetic distances across autosomal genomes (b).
Tree (a) topology: (((A1, (A2, (E1, E2))), (N1 (50), N2 (120))), (N3 (400), D1 (90)))
Tree (b) topology: ((A1, (A2, (E1, E2))), (((N1 (50), N2 (120)), N3 (400)), D1 (90)))

Modern humans are represented by 2 African (A1, A2) and 2 Eurasian (E1, E2) individuals.

Archaic hominins are represented by 3 Neanderthals (N1, N2, N3) and one Denisovan (D1).

Numbers in brackets next to archaic hominins indicate the approximate age (in thousands of years ago) of each specimen.

Note: Branch length is arbitrary and conveys no information here.

The split between modern humans and Neanderthals occurred 750-550 thousand years ago.

60-50 thousand years ago, there was a Neanderthal-to-human gene flow event, which occurred in Eurasia (so did not affect African human populations). All non-African modern humans have 2-3% Neanderthal DNA derived from that gene flow event.

However, present-day humans also have sequence segments similar to Neanderthals' because of common human-Neanderthal ancestry, and not just because of gene flow. This phenomenon is called 'Incomplete Lineage Sorting' (ILS).

True or False?

Q.47.1 Neanderthal-like sequences in present-day humans, which result from gene flow, are on average shorter (fewer base pairs long), than those resulting from ILS.

Q.47.2 If branch length in tree b was proportional to the number of accumulated mutations, the branch leading to N2 would be expected to be shorter than the branch leading to N1.

Q.47.3 A possible explanation for the difference between the mitochondrial and autosomal trees, is a gene flow event from humans (populations branching off before A1) to Neanderthals between 400 and 120 thousand years ago, that resulted in human-like mitochondrial DNA being introduced into the gene pool of Neanderthals.

Q.47.4 By combining Neanderthal-like sequence segments from many (>100) unrelated modern humans, one can only recover around 2-3% of the whole Neanderthal genome.

Q.47.5 The maximum frequency of any Neanderthal allele in any present-day non-African population is 3%.

Q.47.6 Neanderthal-like segments in present-day humans are expected to have identical sequences to the corresponding genome segments of the N1 specimen.

Q.47.7 Present day Africans share no alleles in common with Neanderthals.

**Step‑by‑step analysis**

**Q 51.1 – Species R is a C₄ plant and Species Q is a C₃ plant**  
In Figure A the two curves represent a C₄ and a C₃ plant. The C₄ plant has the lower CO₂ compensation point (≈ 0–10 ppm) and a steeper initial rise in net photosynthesis. The curve labelled **b** (species R) is the one that shows the lower compensation point and the higher assimilation at low Cᵢ, whereas the curve labelled **c** (species Q) shows the higher compensation point typical of a C₃ plant. Therefore the statement is **true**.

**Q 51.2 – At 400 ppm Cᵢ the net CO₂ assimilation of plant R is limited by RuBisCO**  
At 400 ppm the intercellular CO₂ in a C₄ plant is already well above the saturation point for RuBisCO because of the CO₂‑concentrating mechanism. Consequently the limitation at this concentration is normally the capacity for RuBP regeneration, not the carboxylation capacity of RuBisCO. Hence the statement is **false** for species R (which is C₄).

**Q 51.3 – At 700 ppm Cᵢ both plants are limited by RuBP regeneration**  
When Cᵢ is raised to 700 ppm, RuBisCO is saturated in both C₃ and C₄ pathways. The next limiting step is the regeneration of RuBP (or, at even higher concentrations, triose‑phosphate utilisation). This is the generally accepted limitation for both plant types at 700 ppm, so the statement is **true**.

**Q 51.4 – At ambient CO₂ (≈ 400 ppm) plant R has a greater photosynthetic water‑use efficiency than plant Q**  
C₄ plants possess a CO₂‑concentrating mechanism that allows them to achieve similar photosynthetic rates with partially closed stomata, resulting in higher water‑use efficiency (more CO₂ fixed per unit water transpired) compared with C₃ plants. Since R is the C₄ species, this statement is **true**.

**Q 51.5 – Reducing the O₂ concentration from 20 % to 2 % would shift the Cᵢ response curve of plant Q leftward, toward that of plant R**  
Lowering O₂ suppresses photorespiration in C₃ plants, decreasing the CO₂ compensation point and increasing net assimilation at a given Cᵢ. This moves the C₃ curve leftward, making it resemble the C₄ curve. Plant Q is the C₃ species, so the described shift would indeed occur, making the statement **true**.

turns.question:
Scientists studied how water stress intensity affects the relationship between photosynthesis and phloem transport (translocation) rate.

Figure 1 shows the relative effects of water stress on photosynthesis and translocation in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor). It is a dual-axis line graph with the following features:
- The x-axis (X) represents Leaf water potential (MPa), with values shown from -1.5 to -2.5 (and extending further negative to approximately -2.8). Note that more negative values indicate more severe water stress.
- The left y-axis (Y) represents Photosynthesis rate ($\mu mol ^{14}CO_2 m^{-2} s^{-1}$), with grid lines at 30, 40, and 50.
- The right y-axis (Z) represents Phloem transport rate (percent $^{14}C$ removed per hour), with grid lines at 20, 25, 30, and 35.
- Curve A (Photosynthesis) is plotted against the left y-axis (Y). It shows a steady decline as leaf water potential becomes more negative. At X = -1.5 MPa, Y is approximately 42. At X = -2.0 MPa, Y is approximately 30. At X = -2.5 MPa, Y is approximately 26. At X = -2.7 MPa, Y is approximately 25.
- Curve B (Phloem transport) is plotted against the right y-axis (Z). It remains relatively stable at mild water stress and then declines at more severe stress. At X = -1.5 MPa, Z is approximately 35. It stays near 34-35 until X reaches approximately -2.0 MPa. As X becomes more negative than -2.0 MPa, Z declines more steeply, reaching approximately 28 at X = -2.5 MPa and 21 at X = -2.7 MPa.

## True Or False?

Q. 52.1 Decreased water potential in the phloem during water stress may inhibit the movement of assimilates because phloem transport depends on turgor.

Q. 52.2 Decreased consumption of assimilates in the sink organs could not be the cause in the decrease in phloem transport of photosynthate exported from leaves during severe water stress.

Q. 52.3 Severe water stress (leaf water potentials of -2.7 MPa), did not completely inhibit photosynthesis.

Q. 52.4 Photosynthesis is more sensitive to water stress compared to phloem transport.

Q. 52.5 The effect of different levels of water stress in different parts of the root system on transport of assimilates, favours root expansion into more moist patches of soil.

Curve B (Phloem transport) remains relatively flat from -1.5 MPa to -2.0 MPa, then decreases more sharply from -2.0 MPa to -2.7 MPa.

Leaves, with or without extrafloral nectaries (EFNs), from six tropical savanna species in Brazil were investigated. Herbivory (% of leaf area eaten) and specific leaf area - SLA (leaf area vs leaf weight) were measured.

EFNs provide food to reward patrolling ant 'guards'. Plants without EFNs have tougher leaves.

Plants with EFNs are: Heteropterys umbellata (I), Banisteriopsis campestris (III) and Peixotoa tomentosa (II)
Plants without EFNs are: Byrsonima coccolobifolia (VI), Byrsonima verbascifolia (IV) and Byrsonima intermedia (V)

**Figure 1. Herbivory levels.**
In the right panel, plant species were grouped according to presence or absence of EFNs. Lines within bars represent the median and dots represent outliers. Bars labelled with the same lowercase letters (a and b) are not significantly different from each other.
Y-axis: Herbivory (%) levels
X-axis: Plant species (I to VI) and grouped (VII, VIII)
- I (H. umbellata): median ~3.5, label 'a'
- II (P. tomentosa): median ~4.0, label 'a'
- III (B. campestris): median ~5.0, label 'a'
- IV (B. verbascifolia): median ~10.5, label 'b'
- V (B. intermedia): median ~9.0, label 'b'
- VI (B. coccolobifolia): median ~11.0, label 'b'
- VII (Plants with EFNs): median ~4.0, label 'a'
- VIII (Plants without EFNs): median ~10.5, label 'b'
(Left panel ANOVA: F_{5,84} = 11.299, P < 0.0001. Right panel ANOVA: F_{1,88} = 53.203, P < 0.0001)

**Figure 2. Specific Leaf Area.**
(Note the order of I to VI on the x-axis)
Bars labelled with the same lowercase letters (a, b, c) are not significantly different from each other.
Y-axis: SLA (mm^2 mg^-1)
X-axis: Plant species (II, III, I, V, IV, VI) and grouped (VII, VIII)
- II (P. tomentosa): median ~10.2, label 'a'
- III (B. campestris): median ~7.2, label 'b'
- I (H. umbellata): median ~7.5, label 'b'
- V (B. intermedia): median ~6.5, label 'b'
- IV (B. verbascifolia): median ~6.5, label 'bc'
- VI (B. coccolobifolia): median ~5.5, label 'c'
- VII (Plants with EFNs): median ~8.2, label 'a'
- VIII (Plants without EFNs): median ~6.2, label 'b'
(Left panel ANOVA: F_{5,84} = 24.236, P < 0.0001. Right panel ANOVA: F_{1,88} = 36.973, P < 0.0001)

Figure 1. Time course of radial growth increment (increase) of untapped and tapped trees. Filled horizontal bars show the tapping period. Vertical bars indicate the standard error for each month.
[Graph description: A line graph with X-axis "Months and year" (Nov-01 to May-03) and Y-axis "Radial increment (mm)" (-1 to 9). A filled horizontal bar at the bottom indicates the tapping period (W), which runs from Nov-01 to Apr-02, and from Jun-02 to Apr-03. There is a non-tapping period between Apr-02 and Jun-02. Two lines are shown: A (Untapped) and B (Tapped). From Dec-01 to Apr-02, both A and B show near-zero radial increment. Untapped trees (A) show continuous rapid radial growth from Jun-02 to Nov-02 (reaching ~6.5 mm), then plateau from Dec-02 to Mar-03 at ~7 mm. Tapped trees (B) show much slower growth from Jun-02 onwards, reaching ~2.5 mm by Aug-02 and plateauing at ~3.5 mm from Dec-02 to Mar-03.]

Figure 2. Fine-scale measurement of stem diameter variation of untapped control trees.
[Graph description: A scatter plot with X-axis showing dates from 31 May 02 to 6 Jun 02 (vertical grid lines indicate the start of each day at midnight) and Y-axis "Trunk Radius Variation (μm) - untapped tree" (W) ranging from 950 to 1150. - Contraction phase (B): The trunk radius decreases. This phase occurs in the hours following the midnight grid line (roughly the first half of the day).
- Recovery phase (C): The trunk radius increases. This phase occurs in the hours preceding the next midnight grid line (roughly the second half of the day).
- Trunk radius increment (A): The trunk radius reaches a new peak. This phase occurs around the midnight grid lines (spanning late night to early morning).]

Q. 56.1 Rubber trees normally only show radial growth from the onset of the rainy season (April) until the onset of the dry season (November). (1.0 pt)

Q. 56.2 Until tapping was resumed, the growth dynamics of tapped and untapped trees were similar. (1.0 pt)

Q. 56.3 Trunk radius shows an increment (increase) in the daytime, and a contraction in the night-time. (1.0 pt)

Q. 56.4 The daily variations in stem diameter would be a consequence of variations in stem water content. (1.0 pt)

Q. 56.5 The effect of tapping on radial growth rate shows very strong competition for carbon between the artificial sink (latex production) with the naturally dominant sink (trunk growth). (1.0 pt)
